title: A Vista of NGC 2626 with the SMARTS 0.9-meter Telescope
caption: The reflection nebula NGC 2626, imaged by the SMARTS 0.9-meter Telescope
credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/SMARTS Consortium. Image processing: T. A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), M. Zamani & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: NGC 2626 looks vivid enough to pass for a painting, but this is a real picture of the reflection nebula, which lies in the direction of Vela, 3300 light-years from Earth. Red patches of nebulosity within it are glowing hydrogen gas.

A reflection nebula gives off no light of its own. Instead, its dust particles scatter light from one or more nearby stars back toward us. Blue light scatters more efficiently than red, so reflection nebulae often take on a bluish tint.

That is the same physics that turns Earth's daytime sky blue, as sunlight scatters in our atmosphere. The observations behind this image were made with the SMARTS 0.9-meter Telescope, which operates at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO), part of NSF NOIRLab.
scale: NGC 2626 lies 3300 light-years from Earth, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: Taken with the SMARTS 0.9-meter Telescope at CTIO through g, r, i and hydrogen-alpha filters. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures gather far more light than the eye, so the nebula's blue and red colors appear far stronger than they would through a telescope.
